title: From a Blender scene to a physics simulation

lines.speaker: A
lines.text: Picture a scene you've built in Blender: a soft block, a metal plate, a little contact between them. You want to know how it actually deforms. Normally that means leaving Blender and juggling files and command lines.

lines.speaker: B
lines.text: Which sounds like a lot of switching between tools. Is there a shortcut?

lines.speaker: A
lines.text: That's exactly what PolyFEMBlenderPlugin is for. It's an experimental Blender extension that turns your selected objects, their materials and the contact settings into a setup file for PolyFEM, a finite-element solver. Then it runs the simulation without you leaving Blender.

lines.speaker: A
lines.text: He wrote it for the simulation work at the ÉTS lab. It's meant for people who prepare their scenes in Blender but solve them with PolyFEM. It's published under the ETSim group on GitHub.

lines.speaker: B
lines.text: So what do I actually see inside Blender?

lines.speaker: A
lines.text: A PolyFEM panel in the Physics tab. You pick the objects, give each one elastic properties, either from presets like steel, copper or aluminium, or with your own values. Then there are collapsible sections for contact, time, boundary conditions, the solver and the output.

lines.speaker: B
lines.text: And the meshes themselves? A solver needs a particular kind.

lines.speaker: A
lines.text: Right. The add-on exports each mesh as STL or OBJ, or it can fill it with tetrahedra using TetWild and save it as an MSH file. Then it writes the full PolyFEM setup file, and you can even export only the objects you've selected.

lines.speaker: B
lines.text: Does Blender freeze while the simulation runs?

lines.speaker: A
lines.text: No. PolyFEM runs in a background thread, either through Docker or as a local program, so the interface stays usable. Docker is the default, which means you don't have to install the solver yourself.

lines.speaker: B
lines.text: And when it's done, do you get the results back in the scene?

lines.speaker: A
lines.text: Yes, and that's the nice part. A Render Animation button reads each time step, converts it to a mesh, and keyframes them so the deformation plays back as an animation right in Blender.

lines.speaker: B
lines.text: So the whole loop, scene, solver and playback, lives in one place.

lines.speaker: A
lines.text: Exactly. It needs Blender 4.2 or later, and the written page walks through the installation and the repository layout if you want to try it.
